analysis.one_liner: Shields freight brokers and shippers from lawsuits when a truck they hired causes a crash.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in House committee, despite 15 Republican cosponsors; no Democrat signed on.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped states from holding companies accountable for negligently choosing a trucking company, as long as the company checked three things before hiring: federal registration, minimum required insurance, and no unsatisfactory federal safety rating. It covered brokers, shippers, freight forwarders, warehouses, customs brokers, and other intermediaries that hire motor carriers. It would have applied to every lawsuit filed after enactment, even for crashes that happened earlier.
analysis.who_benefits: Freight brokers, shippers, freight forwarders, warehouses, and other companies that hire trucking firms would gain immunity from negligent-hiring lawsuits. Today, if one of those companies hires a carrier with a record of safety problems and that carrier's truck kills or injures someone, a jury can hold the hiring company responsible for choosing it. Under the bill, a company that ran the three-point federal check within 35 days of pickup could not be sued for that choice, no matter what else it knew or ignored.

how_it_helps.text: Gives hiring companies a federal shield from state-law claims for negligent selection of a motor carrier in personal injury, death, and property damage cases.
Covers a broad list of intermediaries: shippers, brokers, consignees, freight forwarders, ocean and air intermediaries, customs brokers, interchange carriers, and warehouses.
Creates one uniform national hiring standard in place of varying state negligence laws, which supporters would describe as simpler for interstate commerce.

analysis.who_pays: People injured or killed in truck crashes, and their families, would lose the ability to sue the companies that chose the carrier. The three-point check looks backward at paperwork: a carrier could fall out of federal compliance, lose its insurance, or become unsafe after the check, and the hiring company would still be shielded. States would also lose their power to set stricter safety-accountability rules for companies operating on their roads.
analysis.who_pays_short: Truck crash victims and their families

drawbacks.text: A company could be immune even if it hired a carrier it had reason to distrust, because the bill bars liability 'related to the negligent selection' once the three checks are done — the check, not the company's actual care, becomes the legal standard.

The verification window stretches up to 35 days before pickup, so a carrier's registration, insurance, or safety rating could lapse after the check and before the load is hauled, and the hiring company would still be protected.
The immunity would apply to every lawsuit filed after enactment, regardless of when the crash or the conduct causing it occurred, cutting off claims arising from past conduct.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine benefit is predictable: intermediaries would no longer face juries second-guessing carrier choices nationwide, which the freight industry has long sought. But the cost falls directly on the people truck crashes hurt most. A paperwork check is a weak substitute for a jury examining whether a company actually picked a safe carrier, the 35-day window leaves real gaps, and the shield would reach back to claims from crashes that happened before the law passed. On balance, the bill traded victims' legal recourse for a liability shield, and it offered the public little in return — it did not raise the federal safety standards themselves, only the bar for suing those who hired unsafe carriers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees and their subcommittees, but no hearing or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Duncan Jr. of Tennessee introduced the bill on February 26, 2015, joined by Reps. Hanna, Rodney Davis, Paulsen, and Meadows as original cosponsors.
The Speaker referred it to both the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Judiciary Committee.
In its only subsequent action, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit on February 27 and to the Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice on March 31, 2015.
Fifteen Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Crash victims and their families came out ahead: because the bill died, they kept the right to sue brokers and shippers that negligently hire unsafe carriers, and freight intermediaries did not receive the liability shield they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Truck crash victims and their families

industries.industry: Freight brokers, shippers, and logistics intermediaries
industries.note: The bill would hand these companies immunity from negligent-hiring lawsuits for a paperwork check, shifting the cost of crashes they help set in motion onto victims. Their gain would come directly out of victims' legal recourse.

Negligent-hiring claims against brokers and shippers are a core tool for injured crash victims; the bill would eliminate most of that litigation. Its death preserved both victims' claims and this line of work.

With intermediaries shielded after a minimal check, weaker carriers would become easier to hire and harder to hold anyone accountable for. Highway safety would depend entirely on the carriers' own thin federal standards.
